title: Highly Selective Electrocatalytic Reduction of CO2 into Methane on Cu–Bi Nanoalloys
abstract: Methane (CH4), the main component of natural gas, is one of the most valuable products facilitating energy storage via electricity conversion. However, the poor selectivity and high overpotential for CH4 formation with metallic Cu catalysts prevent realistic applications. Introducing a second element to tune the electronic state of Cu has been widely used as an effective method to improve catalytic performance, but achieving high selectivity and activity toward CH4 remains challenging. Here, we successfully synthesized Cu–Bi NPs, which exhibit a CH4 Faradaic efficiency (FE) of as high as 70.6% at −1.2 V vs reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE). The FE of Cu–Bi NPs has increased by approximately 25-fold compared with that of Cu NPs. DFT calculations showed that alloying Cu with Bi significantly decreases the formation energy of *COH formation, the rate-determining step, which explains the improved performance. Further analysis showed that Cu that has been partially oxidized due to electron withdrawal by Bi is the most possible active site. ABSTRACT: Methane (CH4), the main component of natural gas, is one of the most valuable products facilitating energy storage via electricity conversion. However, the poor selectivity and
high overpotential for CH4 formation with metallic Cu catalysts prevent realistic applications. Introducing a second element to tune the electronic state of Cu has been widely used as an effective
method to improve catalytic performance, but achieving high selectivity and activity toward CH4 remains challenging. Here, we successfully synthesized Cu–Bi NPs, which exhibit a CH4 Faradaic efficiency (FE) of as high as 70.6% at −1.2 V vs reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE). The FE of
Cu–Bi NPs has increased by approximately 25-fold compared with that of Cu NPs. DFT
calculations showed that alloying Cu with Bi significantly decreases the formation energy of
*COH formation, the rate-determining step, which explains the improved performance. Further
analysis showed that Cu that has been partially oxidized due to electron withdrawal by Bi is the
most possible active site.

KEYWORDS CO2 reduction reaction; Cu alloy; methane; DFT; faraday efficiency;
The electrochemical reduction of CO2 into value-added products provides an attractive strategy for reducing atmospheric CO2 concentrations. 1-7 Intensive studies focusing on metal-based electrocatalysts for the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) have been conducted to distinguish candidates that are capable of reducing CO2 into value-added chemicals, such as CO, 8, 9 HCOOH,10, 11 CH4, 12, 13 C2H4, 14, 15 and C2H5OH 16. Cu is the only pure metal catalyst that is known to electrochemically convert CO2 into appreciable amounts of hydrocarbons, such as CH4 and C2H4. Modifying Cu to achieve high activity and stability with exclusive selectivity for a single class of target hydrocarbons is of great interest.
Considerable progress has been made toward improving catalytic performance in the reduction of CO2 on Cu-based electrodes. 17 The selectivity for the production of C2+ species in CO2RR has been greatly enhanced by tuning the effects of particle size,18 surface structure,19 oxidation state,20 grain boundaries,21 crystal facets,22 and components23 on the performance of Cu electrocatalysts, especially the introduction of Cu2O compositions. 14, 15, 18, 24, 25

Alloying has been proven to be a powerful method for tailoring the electronic properties of metal
catalysts; it is based on synergistic effects that can break the scaling relationship to enhance reaction directionality toward a specific hydrocarbon.26 Various Cu-based binary electrocatalysts, such as Au–Cu,27 Cu–Pd,28 and Cu–In alloy,29 for the CO2RR have been synthesized. These electrodes exhibit improved catalytic performances compared with pure metals. CO is the major product of most Cu-based alloys in most cases.30 Achieving high
selectivity for CH4 over Cu is desired but remains a massive challenge.
CH4 is the main component of natural gas and an important energy storage medium with high energy density owing to its high H content (25 wt%). However, the poor selectivity of CH4 production through CO2 reduction prevents its further industrial utilization. The reaction pathway toward CH4 production requires the addition of a proton to the *CO intermediate to generate *CHO or *COH.31 However, activated protons also tend to combine with each other to produce
H2, competing with the formation of CH4. *CO is a quite stable intermediate that requires extensive energy to be protonated. As a result, few catalysts have good selectivity for CH4 production.
Herein, we develop a novel Cu–Bi bimetallic nanocatalyst that presents high efficiency and
selective activity for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 into CH4. Charge transfer occurs within Cu and Bi elements such that the Cu in Cu–Bi is promoted to the Cu1+ valence state. The electronic property and CO2RR performance of the Cu 1+ in Cu–Bi are significantly different from those of the Cu1+ in Cu2O. This feature accounts for the 25-fold enhancement in the ratio of CH4 to the competing C2H4 products shown by the Cu–Bi nanoalloy compared with that exhibited by pure Cu. This ratio is the highest among currently reported Cu-based CO2RR catalysts.

Cu–Bi bimetallic nanoparticles (NPs) were prepared through a facile one-step method by using
copper nitrate and bismuth nitrate as precursors and sodium borohydride as the reductant (see SI
for experimental details). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images show that the as-
synthesized Cu–Bi NPs have a core diameter of approximately 5 nm and interconnected
dendritic morphologies (Figures 1 and S1–S5). Cu–Bi NPs with similar morphologies and
particles sizes can be prepared with various stoichiometric ratios (Cu, Cu9Bi1, Cu7Bi1, Cu3Bi1, and Bi). Thus, the enhancement in CO2RR performance cannot be a size effect. The results of energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy elemental analysis for Cu7Bi1 NPs (Figure 1D) show that the distribution ranges for Cu (red) and Bi (green) almost completely overlap. This close
correlation indicates that Cu and Bi atoms mix randomly within the alloy NPs, forming a solid
solution structure. This feature is consistent with the Cu–Bi phase diagram obtained at room
temperature. The absence of characteristic Bi peaks in the X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of
the Cu–Bi NPs (Figure S6) further confirms the formation of a solid solution wherein Bi atoms
are distributed within the Cu matrix. HRTEM images (Figure S1–S5) and XRD patterns (Figure
S6) show that the lattice distance shifts to a high value as the amount of Bi is increased. This
shift can be attributed to the enhanced amount of Bi within the Cu matrix. Meanwhile, the XRD
peaks of the synthesized samples exhibit broad band width and low intensity, indicating that the
samples have very small particle sizes in agreement with TEM observations.
The electronic structure of heterogeneous catalysts plays a key role in their catalytic activity. To
understand the electronic structure of Cu-based electrocatalysts, we performed X-ray absorption
spectroscopy (XAS). Figure 2A shows the Cu K-edge X-ray absorption near-edge structural
(XANES) spectra of Cu, Cu9Bi1, Cu7Bi1, Cu3Bi1, and Bi NPs. Comparison with the Cu reference spectra clearly indicates that the Cu in these samples is different from CuO and is similar to

the white-line area can be integrated and used to estimate the charge of Cu, as shown in Figure

presence of a slightly oxidized Cu state in the Cu–Bi NPs. With the increase in the Bi fraction,
the peak area increases in the alloys, indicating the transfer of charge from Cu to Bi at the atomic scale.8, 32-34

The k3-weighted and Fourier transformed extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS)
spectra of the Cu7Bi1 NPs and Cu2O reference are presented in Figure 2B. The peak of 1.42 Å is assigned to Cu–O interaction. The peak of 2.72 Å is attributed to Cu–Cu interaction.35 The Cu
FT-EXAFS feature of Cu7Bi1 NPs is different from that of the Cu2O reference, suggesting that

photoemission spectroscopy (XPS) peaks in Figure 2C show the peaks locating at 931.5 eV and
951.0 eV for Cu NPs are shifted to the higher energy of 932.2 eV and 952.1 eV for Cu7Bi1 nanoalloys, respectively. This feature confirms the oxidized state of Cu upon the alloying of Bi
with Cu and is in agreement with the Cu XAS results. In Figure 2D, the Bi 4f peaks for Cu–Bi
alloys shift to a lower energy compared with those for nano-Bi, with the Bi 4f of Cu7Bi1 NPs at the lowest binding energy. Taking the XAS and XPS results together, we conclude that a strong
interaction exists between Cu and Bi within Cu–Bi NPs. In this interaction, electrons are donated from Cu to Bi within the Cu–Bi nanoalloy, leading to a Cu1+ valence feature.
Figure 2. Characterization of the chemical state for the catalysts. (A) Cu K-edge XANES spectra and (B) Cu FT-EXAFS spectra of samples; (C) Cu 2p and (D) Bi 4f XPS spectra of samples.
The CO2 reduction activities of Cu–Bi NPs with various Cu/Bi atomic ratios were determined by performing constant potential electrolysis in 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte saturated with CO2. The

Cu and Cu–Bi NPs reduce CO2 into multiple products, including CH4, C2H4, CO, and HCOOH (Figure S8). Bi NPs convert CO2 into HCOOH and CO. All these processes are accompanied by the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER).
The Cu alloyed with Bi sharply increases CH4 selectivity and activity with the following notable observations:
• As-synthesized Cu NPs produce CH4 with an onset potential of −0.7 V versus the reversible
hydrogen electrode (RHE, hereafter all the potentials mentioned are referenced to RHE) and
reach a peak Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 20.7% at −1.2 V (Figure 3A).
• Cu9Bi1 NPs yield a peak CH4 FE of 45.1% at −1.2 V.
• For Cu7Bi1 NPs, the maximum CH4 FE reaches 70.6% at −1.2 V.
• The selectivity for CH4 formation decreases with further increases in the amounts of Bi in the
Cu–Bi alloy, such as Cu3Bi1, leading to the FE of 14.7% at the potential of −1.2 V.
Among the Cu–Bi NPs, Cu7Bi1 NPs have the lowest onset potential at −0.6 V. C2H4 yield is also sensitive to the amount of Bi in the alloy (Figure 3B). The increased amount of Bi in the alloy
decreases the production of C2H4. The alloying of Bi with Cu is also beneficial for reducing H formation. The Cu7Bi1 NPs have the best performance for suppressing the HER (Figure 3C). Figure 3D shows the FE ratios of CH4/C2H4 at various applied potentials for four kinds of Cu–Bi NPs. Compared with pure Cu NPs, all Cu–Bi NPs show very high selectivity for CH4 formation. Compared with that of pure Cu NPs, the selectivity of Cu7Bi1 NPs is enhanced 25-fold in terms of the ratio of CH4 to competing C2H4 at the applied potential of –1.2 V and is far higher than

The CH4 partial current densities (jCH4) of different NPs are shown in Figure 3F. The Cu7Bi1 NPs possess the highest jCH4 over the applied cathode potential range of −0.6 V to −1.3 V. Its jCH4 reaches 37.8 mA/cm2 at −1.2 V. By contrast, the jCH4 of pure Cu NPs is 9.5 mA/cm 2 at −1.2 V. Thus, the CH4 partial current densities of Cu7Bi1 NPs has increased by 4-fold relative to that of sole Cu. As shown in Figure S9, the Cu7Bi1 NPs also present significantly improved stability compared with Cu NPs. The alloying of Bi with Cu dramatically prolongs the lifetime of Cu-
based catalysts.
We carried out density functional theory (DFT) calculations to investigate the reaction
mechanism of CO2 reduction on Cu and Cu7Bi1 NPs by calculating the formation energy of key intermediates. Cu(111) was utilized to simulate Cu NPs. Cu7Bi1 (111) was constructed by replacing one Cu with Bi in the Cu primitive cell and used to simulate Cu7Bi1 NPs (additional details regarding the simulation models are presented in the SI). Our previous work 41 indicates
that either *COH formation or *CHO formation is the potential rate-determining step that is
dependent on the Cu facet. The formation energy of *COH (ΔE*COH) is:
ΔE*COH = E*COH – (E*CO + 0.5*EH2) (1)
The formation energy of *CHO(ΔE*CHO) is:
ΔE*COH = E*CHO – (E*CO + 0.5*EH2) (2)
Here, E*COH, E*CHO, and E*CO are the potential energies of *COH, *CHO, and CO predicted from DFT calculations. In our calculations, we found that the formation energy of *CHO on
Cu7Bi1 is 0.81 eV, and the formation energy of *COH is 0.77 eV. Therefore, the formation energy of *COH is 0.04 eV lower than that of *CHO, indicating that *COH is highly likely to be

the first reduction product on Cu7Bi1 NPs. Meanwhile, we carried out free energy calculations to predict the reaction barriers and found that the free energy barrier of *COH formation is 0.89 eV
while the free energy barrier of *CHO formation is 1.02 eV. Therefore, we concluded that the
formation of *CHO is kinetically blocked. The optimized atomic structures of *COH on Cu7Bi1 NPs and Cu NPs are shown in Figures 4A to D.
Figure 4. The optimized atomic structures of *COH on Cu from side view (A) and top view (C), on Cu7Bi1 from side view (B) and top view (D), (E) formation energy of *COH (in eV) of Cu and Cu7Bi1, and *CHO on Cu7Bi1. The colors are Cu in orange, C in gray, O in red, and H in white.
We also investigated the formation energies of *CHOH, *CH, *CH2, and *CH3, which are essential reactive intermediates of CH4 formation. All the formation energies of these products are less than 0.77 eV, indicating that *COH formation is the potential determining step (PDS) in
CH4 formation on Cu7Bi1 NPs. The complete reaction pathway of CH4 formation is in SI. We also calculated that the formation energy of *COH on Cu is 1.03 eV. This value is consistent

with our previously reported value. Thus, introducing Bi into Cu does not change the reaction
mechanism but significantly decreases the formation energy of *COH, which determines PDS.
This effect explains the experimental observations indicating that Cu7Bi1 NPs exhibit improved performance in CO2RR into CH4. Lowdin population analysis shows a 0.13 e − transfer from Cu to Bi that dramatically influences the chemical binding of this intermediate to the catalyst
surface. This result is consistent with the results of the above XAS analysis.
C2 formation potentially competes with C1 formation. Thus, we also consider the formation
energy of *OC-COH, the widely accepted potential determining step of C2 formation, in our
simulation. Our prediction showed that the formation energy of *OC-COH is 0.91 eV, very close
to the previous predictions of 0.95 eV. Considering that the formation energy of *COH is 0.77
eV, it is likely that CO can be directly reduced to CH4 instead of waiting for another CO to couple to form a C2 product. Our prediction is consistent with experimental observations.
Meanwhile, the surface net charge and hydrogen bond (HB) network have been demonstrated to have influence on the DFT predications42, 43. we have included the solvation effect and HB by
including both implicit solvation model and one explicit water, which represents the minimal
simulation model with both effects the hydrogen bond network. Our simulation results show that
the formation energy for *CO to *COH, which all with on explicit water and implicit solvation
model, is 0.605eV. Thus, with consideration of solvation and HB interaction, the formation of
*COH is further stabilized by 0.165 eV, making the CH4 formation through *COH is more favorable, which is consistent with the gas phase prediction.
In summary, we successfully synthesized a Cu–Bi bimetallic nanocatalyst with improved activity
and selectivity for the electrochemical transformation of CO2 into CH4. Compared with pure Cu NPs, the Cu7Bi1 NPs show selectivity at −1.2 V for CH4 over C2H4 that has been enhanced by

25-fold and CH4 partial current densities that have been enhanced by 4-fold. DFT calculations suggested that introducing Bi significantly decreases the formation energy of the PDS of CO2 into CH4. This effect explains the improvement in CH4 activity and selectivity. Further analysis demonstrated that the highly electropositive Bi withdraws electron from Cu, resulting in partially
oxidized Cu, which is the most likely active site for CO2RR into CH4. These results provide insight into the rational design of efficient Cu-based alloy catalysts for the conversion of CO2 into specific products.
